title: "Day 1 — The 7 Patterns of R (and Python's Zen)"
subtitle: "Week 1 · Why R feels chaotic, and the map that fixes it"

## Cheat sheet (30 seconds)

| # | R pattern | One-line recognition cue | Python counterpart |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Vectorization | "no loop, whole vector at once" | numpy / pandas vectorization |
| 2 | The pipe `|>` | "data first, then verbs" | method chaining `.query().assign()` |
| 3 | df-in, df-out | "function eats data.frame, returns data.frame" | functions taking/returning DataFrames |
| 4 | Formula `y ~ x` | "tilde = model spec" | patsy/statsmodels `"mpg ~ am"` |
| 5 | Tidy eval `{{ var }}` | "column names as arguments" | — (plain string/kwargs) |
| 6 | Functionals `map()` | "loop hidden in a function" | comprehensions / `map()` |
| 7 | S3 dispatch | "`plot(x)` does different things per class" | `__repr__`, dunder dispatch |

## Why R feels "too flexible" (10 min)

R is not one language — it's **two dialects welded together**:

- **base R** (S heritage): `attach()`, `sapply()`, `df$x[cond]`, `for` loops, `matrix` stats style
- **tidyverse** (tidy heritage): `dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `tibble`, pipes, consistent naming

Most confusion (including in AI-generated code) comes from **mixing the dialects
mid-script**. The fix used throughout this course:

> ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
> ## Rule 1 of this course
> **Write tidyverse-first.** Learn to *read* base R fluently, but produce
> tidyverse. When you must touch base (modeling internals, bioinformatics
> packages like DESeq2), isolate it in a small function with a tidy wrapper.
> :::

The second source of chaos: R's superpowers — vectorization, formulas,
functional programming, S3 dispatch — are *invisible* if nobody names them.
So here they are, named. **These 7 patterns cover ~90% of good R you will ever
read or write.**

All `{webr}` cells on a page **share one R session**, so `library()` once and
every later cell can use it.

## Pattern 1 — Vectorization

No `for` loop: operate on the whole vector. R's most important idea.

```{webr}
#| label: p1-r
x <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)

x * 2 + 1          # every element, at once
ifelse(x > 4, "hi", "lo")   # vectorized if
sqrt(x)            # every function is vectorized
```

```python
# Python: plain lists can't do this...
import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 4, 6, 8])

x * 2 + 1
np.where(x > 4, "hi", "lo")
np.sqrt(x)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## R vs Python indexing heads-up
R vectors are **1-indexed**; numpy arrays are **0-indexed**. Full table in
[Day 2](day2-data-structures.qmd).
:::

## Pattern 2 — The pipe (data first)

```{webr}
#| label: p2-r
library(dplyr)

mtcars |>
  filter(cyl != 4) |>
  group_by(cyl) |>
  summarise(mean_mpg = mean(mpg))
```

Read it as a sentence: *"take mtcars, **then** filter, **then** group, **then**
summarise."* The pipe works because every dplyr verb takes the data frame as
its **first argument**. That's Pattern 3 hiding inside Pattern 2.

```python
# Python: the same "sentence" is method chaining
import pandas as pd
mtcars = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vincentarelbundock/Rdatasets/master/csv/datasets/mtcars.csv")

(mtcars
   .query("cyl != 4")
   .groupby("cyl")["mpg"]
   .mean())
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## AI-code smell
`mtcars <- filter(mtcars, cyl != 4)` repeated five times with five different
names (`mtcars2`, `mtcars3`, `df_final`, `df_final2`...) — that's pipe-less
tidyverse. Refactor into one `|>` chain.
:::

## Pattern 3 — df-in, df-out functions

```{webr}
#| label: p3-r
library(dplyr)

summarise_cyl <- function(df, min_mpg = 0) {
  df |>
    filter(mpg >= min_mpg) |>
    group_by(cyl) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean_mpg = mean(mpg))
}

summarise_cyl(mtcars, min_mpg = 15)
```

The shape is always: **data in → pipeline → data out**. One function = one
verb-sized transformation. Compose them like Lego.

```python
def summarise_cyl(df, min_mpg=0):
    return (df[df["mpg"] >= min_mpg]
              .groupby("cyl")["mpg"]
              .agg(["count", "mean"])
              .reset_index())
```

## Pattern 4 — The formula interface

The tilde is R's mini-language for "left side explained by right side."

```{webr}
#| label: p4-r
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
summary(fit)$coefficients
```

You will meet formulas everywhere: `lm`, `glm`, `boxplot(mpg ~ cyl)`,
`DESeq2` designs (`~ batch + condition`), `edgeR`, mixed models. **Formulas
are the single most reused syntax in applied R statistics** — worth loving.

```python
# Python borrowed the exact idea (patsy formula language)
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
fit = smf.ols("mpg ~ wt + C(cyl)", data=mtcars).fit()
fit.params
```

## Pattern 5 — Tidy eval: `{{ }}` (recognize, don't memorize)

When a function takes a *column name* as an argument, dplyr needs `{{ }}`
to look inside it:

```{webr}
#| label: p5-r
library(dplyr)

group_mean <- function(df, group_col, value_col) {
  df |>
    group_by({{ group_col }}) |>
    summarise(mean = mean({{ value_col }}))
}

group_mean(mtcars, cyl, mpg)
```

You mostly need to **recognize** `{{ }}` (so AI-generated wrappers stop
looking alien). Reach for it when your own functions take column names.

## Pattern 6 — Functionals (loops in disguise)

```{webr}
#| label: p6-r
library(purrr)

genes <- list(A = c(3, 5, 8), B = c(1, 9), C = c(4, 4, 4, 4))

map_dbl(genes, mean)          # named vector of means
map_int(genes, length)        # named vector of lengths
```

Rule of thumb: `map()` for transformation, `walk()` for side-effects
(plots, saves). Inside dplyr, the same idea appears as `across()` and
`group_modify()`.

```python
genes = {"A": [3, 5, 8], "B": [1, 9], "C": [4, 4, 4, 4]}
{k: sum(v) / len(v) for k, v in genes.items()}   # comprehension = map
```

## Pattern 7 — S3 dispatch (why `summary()` is psychic)

`summary()`, `plot()`, `print()` behave differently depending on the **class**
of the object. That's S3: one generic function, many per-class methods.

```{webr}
#| label: p7-r
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
class(fit)          # "lm"
names(methods(plot))[1:5]   # dozens of plot.<class> methods exist
```

```python
# Python: the same concept is dunder methods + classes
# print(obj)  calls obj.__str__
# len(obj)    calls obj.__len__
# df.head()   is a method on the DataFrame class
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## This pays off in bioinformatics
`DESeqDataSet`, `Seurat` objects, `phyloseq`, `SummarizedExperiment` — all are
S3/S4 objects. When `plot(x)` "just works" on them, you now know why, and
you know to look for `methods(class = "DESeqDataSet")` to discover the API.
:::

## Read & refactor: AI code in the wild

Real pattern: chatbot-generated R that *works* but teaches you nothing.
Diagnose it with the 7 patterns:

```r
# ❌ Before: valid R, zero patterns
result <- c()
for (i in 1:length(mtcars$cyl)) {
  if (mtcars$cyl[i] > 4) {
    result[i] <- mtcars$mpg[i] * 1.1
  } else {
    result[i] <- mtcars$mpg[i]
  }
}
mtcars$mpg_adj <- result
```

What's wrong? (click)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The diagnosis
1. `1:length(...)` is a **real bug** — if the vector is empty this becomes
   `1:0` = `c(1, 0)` and the loop still runs. Use `seq_along()`.
2. Row-wise loop + `if` = Pattern 1 (`ifelse`) begging to be used.
3. Growing a vector in a loop (`result <- c(...)`) is slow and fragile.
4. Direct `df$col[i]` indexing is base dialect; data should flow through a pipe.
:::

```r
# ✅ After: Pattern 1 + Pattern 2, one line of intent
mtcars_adj <- mtcars |>
  mutate(mpg_adj = if_else(cyl > 4, mpg * 1.1, mpg))
```

## Drills (live pad)

Predict each output **before** running. Edit freely — this session is yours.

```{webr}
#| label: drills
library(dplyr)

# 1. Vectorize: convert c(15, 22, 9, 30) °C to °F  (F = C*9/5 + 32)

# 2. ifelse: label mtcars$cyl as "low" (4) / "high" (otherwise)

# 3. Pipe: top 3 rows of mtcars sorted by hp, descending

# 4. map_dbl: mean of each column of mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp", "wt")]

# 5. Formula: boxplot(mpg ~ am, data = mtcars)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers
1. `c(15, 22, 9, 30) * 9 / 5 + 32`
2. `ifelse(mtcars$cyl == 4, "low", "high")`
3. `mtcars |> arrange(desc(hp)) |> slice_head(n = 3)`
4. `map_dbl(mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp", "wt")], mean)`
5. `boxplot(mpg ~ am, data = mtcars)` — a formula, not a loop
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 — vectorize the loop

Rewrite `classify_gc()` **without** any loop or `if`, using vectorization.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d1-vector
classify_gc <- function(gc_scores, threshold = 50) {
  # Return "high" or "low" for every score, vectorized
  # (gc_scores is like c(39.2, 55.1, 48.7, 61.0))
  ______
}

classify_gc(c(39.2, 55.1, 48.7, 61.0))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d1-vector"}
`if_else(condition, "high", "low")` or `ifelse()` — one call, whole vector.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d1-vector"}
```r
classify_gc <- function(gc_scores, threshold = 50) {
  if_else(gc_scores > threshold, "high", "low")
}
```
:::

### Exercise 2 — build a pipe

Using `mtcars`: keep rows with `wt > 2`, then for each `cyl` compute
`n` and `mean_wt`, sorted by `mean_wt` descending. One pipe.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d1-pipe
library(dplyr)

heavy_summary <- mtcars |>
  ______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d1-pipe"}
Verbs in order: `filter()` → `group_by()` → `summarise(n = n(), mean_wt = mean(wt))` → `arrange(desc(mean_wt))`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d1-pipe"}
```r
heavy_summary <- mtcars |>
  filter(wt > 2) |>
  group_by(cyl) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_wt = mean(wt)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_wt))
```
:::

### Exercise 3 — the pattern audit

For each line, name the pattern (1–7):

```r
a) ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
b) purrr::map(files, read_csv)
c) df |> mutate(z = x / sum(x))
d) DESeq(dds)                      # thinks about: dds is an S4 object
e) coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age, data = df)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

a) none directly (grammar of graphics, but data flows in as first arg — P2/P3 spirit)
b) Pattern 6 · c) Pattern 2 · d) Pattern 7 · e) Pattern 4
:::
